blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Rad-Linter checks chest X-ray reports against image-derived evidence to flag potential errors for review. A pretrained image classifier supplies scores for nine pathologies, and a 1.5B-parameter language model, fine-tuned with LoRA on 1,816 examples, checks their consistency with the report. We compare it with a keyword-and-negation rule baseline given the same reports and scores. Evaluation uses controlled report-score pairings from OpenI, with consistency labels derived from automatic report labels and score thresholds. Each counterfactual quad crosses two real reports with two real score vectors from other patients, creating two consistent and two inconsistent pairs. Every report and score vector occurs in both conditions, so either input alone permits only 50% accuracy. On 131 quads, Rad-Linter achieves 98.5% pair accuracy versus 80.5% for the rule baseline, and classifies all four pairs correctly in 94.4% of quads versus 56.5%. The checkers perform similarly on omission items, including unmentioned and negated findings; larger differences occur on the remaining item types, which require interpreting how findings are described. The same language model without fine-tuning remains near 50% accuracy. On a second set of 181 quads that also includes reports on which the automatic labelers disagree, pair accuracy is 93.4% versus 75.3%. These controlled results show that, given the same image-derived scores, a trained language model detects report-score inconsistencies more accurately than the tested rule baseline, with the advantage concentrated in interpreting how findings are worded.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
A chest X-ray report describes what a radiologist sees in an image
so that other clinicians can use those findings in patient care.
Errors in the report can affect later decisions, which motivates
checking the report before it is acted on ( Brady et al., 2012 ; Bruno et al., 2015 ; Waite et al., 2017 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) .
Some errors cannot be found in the text alone. A report can leave
out a finding or describe one that the image does not support,
yet contain no contradiction between its sentences ( Kim and Mansfield, 2014 ; Itri et al., 2018 ; Patra et al., 2021 ; Hanna et al., 2018 ; Lee et al., 2013 ) .
For example, a report may never mention an effusion even when there
is evidence of one in the image. To check this potential omission,
a reviewer needs evidence about the image as well as the report.

A measurement typo or a disagreement between the detailed findings
and the report’s summary may be detectable this way. Checking a
statement against the image requires an additional source of

blocks.en:
We develop Rad-Linter to make that comparison. First, an image
classifier, a model trained to recognize abnormalities in chest
X-rays, produces one score for each of nine findings, or pathologies ( Rajpurkar et al., 2017 ; Irvin et al., 2019 ; Cohen et al., 2022 ) .
A higher score indicates stronger support from that classifier for
the finding. A language model then receives the report and these
scores and flags potential disagreements. A high effusion
score paired with a report that does not affirm effusion is one
example. Multimodal checkers can instead receive the image and
report directly ( Zou et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) .
Here, the language model receives scores rather than image pixels.
This makes the evidence supplied to it explicit and lets us test
its response when that evidence changes. Our clinical aim is to
identify problems worth reviewing. The task evaluated here is to
detect disagreement between the report and the supplied scores.
Either source may be wrong, and the checker may misread the report;
a clinician must review a flag before treating it as a report error.

blocks.en:
We use a language model because the comparison depends on how a
finding is described. The same pathology name may occur in
“effusion is present,” “no effusion,” or “possible effusion.”
A keyword match alone does not distinguish those meanings. Rules
can add checks for negation and uncertainty, but the relevant words
may be far apart. In “no evidence of consolidation, pneumothorax,
or pleural effusion,” the negation applies to all three findings.
A report may also express uncertainty in one sentence and affirm
the finding in another. We therefore fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B, a
language model with 1.5 billion learned parameters, on this comparison
task.
Fine-tuning means further training an existing model on examples of
the desired input and answer. We use low-rank adaptation
(LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , which trains a small set of added weights
while leaving the model’s original weights fixed.

checker using only one input must give the same answer to two pairs
with opposite reference labels, so it can be correct on only half.

as the presence of any high score, without matching individual
findings.

blocks.en:
We build these tests from OpenI, a public collection of chest
X-rays and reports ( Demner-Fushman et al., 2016 ) . A rule-based reference
labeler assigns report states, which are combined with score
thresholds to generate the test answers. An agreement labeler,
implemented with another language model, provides a second reading
to select primary-test reports on which the readings agree.
On 131 quads, Rad-Linter correctly classifies 98.5% of individual
pairs as consistent or inconsistent, compared with 80.5% for the
rule baseline.
The two perform similarly on the Omission category,
which includes both unmentioned and negated findings paired with
high scores. Larger differences occur in the other item types,
which require interpreting how a finding is stated.
The same language model without task-specific training remains
near 50% accuracy. On a second test set that includes reports on
which the automatic labelers disagree, the trained model retains
an advantage, with 93.4% accuracy against 75.3%.
These results motivate examining the language component of report
checking while holding the image evidence constant. Prior work on
report review, image evidence, and test design provides the basis
for this comparison.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Text-based report review uses language to find problems within a
report. Rule systems match keywords and
patterns ( Donnelly et al., 2022 ; Chng et al., 2023 ) , while neural
systems support error detection and finding
classification ( Min et al., 2022 ; Banerjee et al., 2023 ) .
RadCLARE applies automated review across an
institution ( Pan et al., 2025 ; Devlin et al., 2019 ) . Casey et al. (2021) review natural language processing,
meaning automated analysis of language, in radiology; Nobel et al. (2022) review structured reporting, which uses
predefined report fields. Language models offer another way to
read reports. Gertz et al. (2024) inserted 150 textual errors into
100 of 200 reports and found GPT-4 close to radiologists at detecting
them. Later studies evaluated closed and open
models ( Salam et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) and errors from
speech recognition ( Schmidt et al., 2024 ) .
These studies support automated text review. Our task additionally
asks whether a statement agrees with evidence outside the report.

Providing two inputs does not ensure that a model uses both.
In natural language inference, a model judges whether one sentence
follows from another. Models can score well even when shown only
the second sentence ( Gururangan et al., 2018 ) .
This is an example of a shortcut: a clue predicts the test answer
without requiring the intended reasoning. Shortcuts have been
studied across deep learning ( Geirhos et al., 2020 ) and in
chest X-ray classification ( Zech et al., 2018 ; DeGrave et al., 2021 ) .
Balanced test pairs help expose them. VQA v2 uses complementary
images for visual questions ( Goyal et al., 2017 ) ; Winoground uses
four image–caption pairings from two images and two
captions ( Thrush et al., 2022 ) ; and symmetric FEVER pairs
balance claims and supporting evidence ( Schuster et al., 2019 ) .
Contrast sets ( Gardner et al., 2020 ) and counterfactually
augmented data ( Kaushik et al., 2020 ) likewise change selected
parts of examples to test whether predictions change appropriately.

blocks.en:
Our task follows the claim–evidence approach of
FEVER ( Thorne et al., 2018 ) and its scientific and health
applications ( Wadden et al., 2020 ; Kotonya and Toni, 2020 ; Sarrouti et al., 2021 ; Guo et al., 2022 ) .
Radiology benchmarks such as ReXErr ( Rao et al., 2025 ) and
CorBenchX create errors by editing reports; synthetic clinical
text is also used in training ( Tang et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2023 ) .
We instead vary the scores paired with unchanged reports.
Following Hessel and Lee (2020) , we also test whether simple
summaries of both inputs can explain performance. These ideas lead
to two requirements for our evaluation: each input alone must be
insufficient, and success must be examined beyond a few broad
clues. The method below defines the inconsistency that the checker
must detect, then builds a comparison that meets these requirements.

blocks.en: 3 Method
blocks.zh: 3 方法

blocks.en: 3.1 What the Checker Detects
blocks.zh: 3.1 国家 检查者检测到什么

blocks.en:
The checker receives one report and a list of image-classifier scores
for nine findings. It returns one judgment: whether the pair is
inconsistent and, if so, the type of disagreement and the affected

blocks.en: 3.5 Additional Checks and Performance Measures

blocks.en:
Our main comparison is Rad-Linter versus the rule baseline. Three
additional checks examine possible explanations for the results.
First, single-input checks receive only the report or only
the scores. They verify the expected behavior of the balanced pairs.

but cannot match a particular finding to its score. Third, the zero-shot model is the same base language model given both
inputs without task-specific fine-tuning. It tests what this model
can achieve from the task description alone. Complete system
identities and settings are in Appendix C .

blocks.en: 5 Discussion
blocks.zh: 5 讨论情况

blocks.en:
The results support using a trained language model to read the
report in a checker supplied with image-classifier scores. Both
checkers receive the same evidence. Their different accuracies
therefore concern the comparison of that evidence with the text.
The gap is small on the Omission category and larger on
the other item types, with differences of 18 to 33 percentage points.
This pattern is consistent with better interpretation of report
wording, including uncertainty and negation. Because each category
contains several kinds of language, a separate analysis of annotated
phrases would be needed to measure the contribution of each kind.

blocks.en:
The practical role of training is clear in this comparison. The
base language model performs poorly without task-specific training,
while the fine-tuned model learns to produce judgments that agree
with the reference answers. Those answers combine states from the
reference labeler with score thresholds. Rad-Linter follows these
conventions more accurately on held-out pairs than the tested rule
baseline, which uses a different report-reading implementation.
This result does not establish an advantage over the procedure
that generates the answers, or over rule-based methods in general.
The agreement labeler helps select the primary reports; its agreement
with the reference labeler does not supply independent clinical truth.

The two-stage design also makes the source of a flag easier to
inspect. The image classifier supplies a score for a finding;
the checker decides whether the report agrees with that score.
Keeping these roles separate lets us hold the image evidence
constant when comparing checkers. It also leaves an interface that
another classifier could supply. Changing the classifier may change
the score distribution, however, so the thresholds and checker
would need to be tested again. Extending the approach to another

its own reports and evidence.

blocks.en: 6 Limitations
blocks.zh: 6 限制

blocks.en:
The labels measure agreement with classifier scores on constructed
pairs. Neither the reference labeler nor the agreement labeler was
validated against clinician judgments, and the agreement labeler
was instructed to use the reference labeler’s conventions.
Agreement between them therefore does not make
the labels a clinical ground truth. We did not compare alternative
report labelers such as CheXbert ( Smit et al., 2020 ) or
RadGraph ( Jain et al., 2021 ) . The image classifier’s training
data also include OpenI, so this study does not test its performance
on an entirely new image collection. A checker may correctly follow
a supplied score even when that score is clinically wrong.

separated between training and test, but identical wording across
those splits was not checked: the 3,599 reports contain only
2,842 distinct texts. Patient separation alone does not rule out
repeated report wording.

We test one model size and one rule baseline. Larger zero-shot
models or stronger rule systems may give different results. The
coarse probe was trained on an earlier set of 303 quads, and no

shortcut. We also changed the training recipe after the initial

below the rule baseline. Revised recipes were compared on a
development split, while the test sets and rule baseline stayed

The study uses one imaging modality and one report collection.
It does not measure whether clinicians make fewer errors or whether

performance separately for patient subgroups. Clinical evaluation
must assess the image evidence and the checker together. The
supported conclusion is the comparison between the two checkers
under the conditions tested here.

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
We developed Rad-Linter to help identify potential errors in
chest X-ray reports by comparing the text with image-classifier
scores. The language model is trained to interpret how each finding
is described and decide whether the report and scores agree.
Using the same evidence as the rule baseline, it correctly classifies
98.5% of pairs as consistent or inconsistent, compared with 80.5%
for that baseline in the primary controlled test. The advantage remains when reports are included
without requiring agreement between automatic labelers. Training
on 1,816 examples is important for the small language model’s
performance on this task.

blocks.en:
The reference labeler is the textlib procedure. It divides
the report into sentences and matches pathology keywords. Its negation
rules extend across a clause, following clinical negation methods
such as NegEx and NegBio ( Chapman et al., 2001 ; Peng et al., 2018 ) .
Semicolons and contrast words can end the scope of a preceding
negation, as can an intervening assertion. The procedure also checks
post-keyword negation and expressions such as “lungs are clear.”
Within a sentence, an applicable negation takes priority over an
uncertainty cue. Across sentences, an affirmation takes priority over
uncertainty, which takes priority over negation; if none is found,
the state is not mentioned. Combining the resulting states with
Appendix A ’s thresholds produces the reference answer.
This procedure supplies training and evaluation labels.

the implementation selects the candidate with the largest distance
beyond its threshold. No candidate yields No_Error .

part of a test quad.

such as “likely atelectasis” or “opacity, may represent pneumonia”

an independently annotated linguistic analysis. The observed pattern
is consistent with the trained model applying the report-labeling
conventions more reliably. Because both checkers receive the same
scores, the difference arises in how they process the supplied
report and evidence, not from access to a better image classifier.

Rad-Linter has two stages: a fixed image classifier supplies the

DenseNet-121 ( Cohen et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2017 ) , a neural network
for image classification, with the public densenet121-res224-all weights ( Cohen et al., 2020 ) .
Those weights were trained on NIH ( Wang et al., 2017 ) ,
PadChest ( Bustos et al., 2020 ) , CheXpert ( Irvin et al., 2019 ) ,
MIMIC-CXR ( Johnson et al., 2019 ) , Google ( Majkowska et al., 2020 ) ,
OpenI ( Demner-Fushman et al., 2016 ) , and RSNA ( Shih et al., 2019 ) .
This choice follows work on chest X-ray
classification ( Rajpurkar et al., 2017 ; Baltruschat et al., 2019 ) and covers all nine findings needed here. We retain nine of its
18 outputs and do not retrain the classifier.

### Task:
Compare the radiology report with the visual evidence and decide whether the report contains an error.
Error types:
- OMISSION: a pathology has strong visual evidence (score >= 0.6) but the report does not affirm it.
- HEDGING: a pathology has strong visual evidence (score >= 0.6) but the report only mentions it with uncertain language.
- CONTRADICTION: a pathology has strong evidence against it (score <= 0.2) but the report affirms it.
- NO_ERROR: none of the above.
Output JSON with fields: has_error (bool), error_type, finding (pathology or null), evidence (string or null), explanation (string).
